name: C13-3
question: Should Hong Kong tighten rent control on subdivided units? Take a position and defend it with evidence from the course archive.

turns.text: I'm looking into how rent regulation affects subdivided flats in Hong Kong—whether capping rents helps tenants or ends up shrinking the market. Could you point me to some sources on this?

You've framed a clear either/or: capping helps tenants versus shrinking the market. Before I point anywhere, which of those two claims would the source need to support — and would it need to show evidence for one side, or a counter-view to test against?

Really both, but the key thing I want to test is whether capping initial rents actually shrinks the supply of subdivided flats—so any evidence on what happens to stock or landlord behaviour under rent controls would be most useful, plus anything on how tenants themselves weigh rent against security.

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D5: Submission: Landlords Association of Hong Kong (Stakeholder submission). Industry association submission speaking for landlords, arguing against hard caps; self-admittedly lacks margin data and relies on a low-response self-reported survey.
- D2: SDU Rent and Stock Index, 2019–2025 (excerpt) (Data excerpt). Statistical data excerpt tracking SDU stock and rents from 2019 to 2025, with a noted caveat on post-2023 survey extrapolation.
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO report presenting a 440-household tenant survey and arguing caps address a price symptom rather than the queue problem.
- D7: Comparative Note: Berlin, Mietendeckel 2020–2021 (Comparative case). Comparative case study of Berlin's 2020–2021 rent freeze, describing supply and market effects before its constitutional annulment.
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper reviewing supply-elasticity literature and modeling a tightened-cap scenario for a Hong Kong-like market.
Pick one or more (by id) and tell me why.

I've read a lot now and want to put the pieces together in my own words before anything else. From the stock index, subdivided unit numbers actually went up from about 107,300 in 2021 to 111,200 in 2025, so the 2021 rules didn't visibly push landlords out. But the academic work separates two kinds of control: older caps on the rent level itself tend to shrink supply, while newer rules limiting increases within a tenancy have small or no stock effect. The modelled Hong Kong case is the worrying one: a 15 percent cut in starting rents helps current tenants by roughly 900 dollars a month but leaves 3,000 to 4,000 households a year unable to get in, mostly new arrivals and newly formed households, who are exactly the people the policy is meant to help. On enforcement, a real initial-rent cap would need a certifiable tenancy register, and that's estimated at 40 to 60 staff-years to build. So my own conclusion is that a light band plus real security of tenure protects the people the current market abandons, without pretending the waiting list is really a rent problem.

You've set out a chain from the stock figures through the two control types to the modelled entry losses, and ended with your own position on a band plus security of tenure. Which of those steps do you see as the load-bearing one — the piece that, if it were weaker, would change your conclusion?

The load-bearing step is the entry-loss figure: if a modest cut in starting rents didn't actually block new households from getting in, the whole case against a hard cap would weaken a lot. The stock index and the two-types distinction matter mostly as context for that.
You've said the entry-loss figure is what the case against a hard cap rests on. What in the modelled Hong Kong case would you want to check to see how firm that 3,000–4,000 a year estimate is?

Good question. I'd want to know what assumptions the model makes about how many new households are trying to enter each year and how sensitive that entry is to the rent level — if it assumes a fixed inflow and a steep response, the 3,000–4,000 could be soft. I'd also like to check whether it lets landlords convert units to storage instead of just exiting, since that would change the number a lot.

You've named two things you'd want to test in the model — the household-entry assumption and whether conversion to storage is allowed. Which single claim in your essay would a source need to support here: that the 3,000–4,000 figure is soft, or something else you're arguing?

None of this is about the entry figure being soft exactly — the point I'm actually making is that a hard cap helps current tenants but pushes the cost onto people trying to get in, and that's why I'd rather tighten tenure first and keep only a light, indexed band on starting rents. The stock numbers and the two-kinds-of-control distinction are just context; they don't prove a binding cap would be harmless. So the claim that needs backing is that the losers from a hard cap are mainly the households still outside, which is exactly the people the policy is meant to help.

Your claim is that the losers from a hard cap are mainly households still outside — the very people the policy aims to help. What would a source need to show for that claim: evidence of who actually gets shut out when a cap binds, or a counter-view arguing the outside households aren't the main losers?

That's the crux. A source would need to show who actually gets shut out when a cap binds — that the households blocked from entering are new arrivals and newly formed households, rather than existing tenants. That's what I'd want to see before leaning on it.

drafts.text: # Tighten, but Not With a Hard Cap: A Case for Tenure Security and a Light Rent Band

# Tighten, but Not With a Hard Cap: A Case for Tenure Security and a Light Rent Band

Hong Kong should tighten regulation of subdivided units (SDUs), but it should not impose a hard cap on initial rents. The archive points toward a narrower package: enforceable security of tenure plus a published, indexed rent band. A hard cap would help some incumbents while shrinking the bottom of the market and failing the very households it is meant to protect. The evidence on stock, enforcement and tenant preferences all points the same way.

The first question is whether tightening would destroy supply. The 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance offers a natural experiment: SDU stock rose from 107,300 units in 2021 to 109,800 in 2023 and 111,200 in 2025, suggesting moderate regulation did not trigger visible exit [D2p1]. But this stability is misleading as a guide to a harder instrument. The 2021 ordinance capped increases within tenancies, not initial rents [D1p3], and the academic literature distinguishes exactly these two designs: first-generation controls on rent levels show consistent contraction, while second-generation controls on increases show small or null effects on stock [D6p2]. The stable stock in the index is therefore evidence that a non-binding instrument does not bind, not that a binding one would be harmless.

How large would contraction be? The reviewed literature estimates long-run supply elasticity for marginal SDU-type stock at 0.31 to 0.48, meaning a 10 percent cap-induced rent cut removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1]. The modelled Hong Kong scenario is starker: a 15 percent cut in initial rents transfers about 900 dollars a month to incumbents but leaves 3,000 to 4,000 households a year unable to enter the segment, mostly new arrivals and newly formed households [D6p4]. Those losers are precisely the population the policy intends to protect [D1p2]. The Berlin case confirms the mechanism: when the Mietendeckel fell, suppressed increases released and new-contract rents jumped above the pre-cap trend [D7p2]. The bill for protecting insiders is handed to those still outside [D7p3].

Tenant evidence complicates the story but does not rescue the hard cap. Mrs Wong supports a hard cap and believes her landlords would never exit, yet she also reports two flats in her stairwell converted to storage after the ordinance—a contradiction she does not see [D4p3]. Mr Chan is more clear-eyed: a cap would free perhaps 800 dollars a month, but he fears landlords would rather convert cubicles to storage than deal with regulated tenants, and he has seen units locked for a year [D3p2]. Asked what would help most, he does not name rent; he names the waiting list [D3p3]. The NGO survey of 440 households reinforces this: 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year tenure security, and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer [D11p1]. The binding constraint is queue length and insecurity, not price.

Enforcement seals the argument. Inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year, and a band-based initial-rent cap would require a certifiable tenancy register costing an estimated 40 to 60 staff-years to build [D10p1]. Worse, the tenants least able to complain—those with no written agreement, like Mrs Wong [D4p1], and the newest arrivals—would be missed first, so enforcement would systematically fail the most exploited tail [D10p2]. The subcommittee could not identify any design under which the newest-arrival tail is protected first rather than last [D10p3]. A hard cap would also invite compensation claims and judicial review, with a litigation timeline outlasting a Council term [D9p1][D9p3].

The alternative is a light band on initial rents, defensible as rate-capping rather than confiscation, paired with real tenure security [D9p2]. The NGO report endorses exactly this narrow tightening and opposes a hard cap on both contraction arithmetic and revealed preference [D11p3]. The government's expected "floor-standard + rent band" package moves in this direction [D12p1]. The objection that the 2021 ordinance's stability proves capacity for more control [D12p2] misreads a non-binding instrument; the counter that a binding cap behaves differently [D12p2] is correct, which is why the band must be indexed, reviewable and backed by an inspection regime before it is imposed.

Tighten, then—but tighten tenure first, and price second. A hard cap protects today's tenants at tomorrow's tenants' expense. A band plus security of tenure protects the tail the current market abandons, without pretending the queue is a rent problem.
